1.

The appellant State, being aggrieved by the judgement and order passed by the Ahmedabad City Sessions Court, Ahmedabad in Sessions Case No. 81 of NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined 1994 on 30.06.1999, whereby, all the accused were acquitted of the charge under Sections 498A and 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code,
has preferred this appeal.

2. The facts as recorded by the court below are that, an F.I.R. was lodged by Rafikabanu - the deceased while she was under treatment at V.S. Hospital, according to which, she was married to accused No.2-Mohmmad Yunus Mohmmadnabi Vora, prior to about one and a half years of the date of incident.

Since about four months prior to the date of the incident, Rafikabanu and her husband - accused No.2, started living separately from her mother- in-law - accused No.1 and the other accused as they frequently used to pick up quarrels with her on trivial matters relating to dowry and gold ornaments.
She was thus treated with cruelty by accused Nos. 1, 2 & 3. 2.1 According to the prosecution

, on the date of the alleged incident, owing to the festival of Bakri Id, the NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined accused no.1 - mother-in-law of deceased as well as accused nos. 3 & 4, sisters-in-law of deceased visited her residence and started instigating accused No.2 - husband of deceased, about inadequate quantity of dowry and her inefficiency in carrying out routine domestic activities.
It is the case of the prosecution that, they instigated accused no.2 to kill Rafikabanu.

Thus, on being instigated by accused nos. 1, 3 & 4, the accused no.2 - husband of Rafikabanu took out a bottle full of acid,
accused nos. 1, 3 & 4 caught hold of Rafikabanu and accused no.2 poured about 3/4th of the acid from the bottle in the mouth of his wife Rafikabanu.
Thus, she was made to ingest acid forcibly, as a result of which, she started vomiting.
Consequently, she was taken to hospital for treatment.
3. The prosecution to bring home the guilt of the accused had examined 6 witnesses and had submitted 8 documents.

Upon completion of the oral evidence, the learned Sessions Judge had recorded the statements of the accused under Section 313 of the Cr.P.C. and after NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined hearing the learned advocates of the either sides, was pleased to pass the order and judgement of acquittal as regards all the accused.
4.

Ms. Jirga Jhaveri, the learned APP submitted that, the impugned judgement is required to be interfered with, inasmuch as, the competent court had erred in not considering the dying declaration, in its true perspective.

She submitted that, out of the six witnesses who were examined,
the dying declaration was made before the mother and brother of the deceased, who have been examined by the prosecution as P.W. 1 and P.W. 2 respectively.
She submitted that, the conduct of accused no. 2 - husband of the deceased was not natural, he having left the hospital after admitting the deceased.
She submitted that, the impugned judgement, therefore is required to be interfered with.

sentences.text: Ms. Urmila Desai, the learned advocate appearing for the respondents - accused supported the impugned NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined judgement rendered by the competent court and submitted that, no interference is called for in the same.

She submitted that, the complaint below Exh. 67 which was subsequently converted to the dying declaration is such that, the same is not believable considering the fact that, the deceased and her husband resided separately for the last four months from the in-laws.
She submitted that, it was the accused no. 2 - husband of the deceased, who had taken her to the hospital for treatment.

5.1 Ms.
Desai placed reliance on the panchnama below Exh. 57 and submitted that, no bottles of acid, either filled or empty, were recovered from the place of incident.
She submitted that, no independent witnesses were examined.

She also placed reliance on the statement of the accused no. 4 recorded under Section 313 of the Cr.P.C wherein it is stated that, at the time of the alleged incident, both the sisters-in-law were at their respective matrimonial houses and that, they were not aware of the incident.

Reliance was also placed on the NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined statement of accused no. 2 given under Section 313 of Cr.P.C wherein it was stated that, when the incident occurred, the accused no. 2 was asleep and it was only after he heard sounds of vomiting that he woke up and thereafter, took the deceased to the hospital.
He had asked a person named Mansuri to inform the deceased's parents.
She submitted that, even the other accused did not have any role in the alleged offence.

6. Having heard learned advocates appearing for the parties and having gone through the impugned judgment coupled with the oral as well as documentary evidence placed on record, it is the prosecution's case that, the deceased Rafikabanu was married to accused No.2 - prior to about one and a half years of the date of incident and that, for about four months before the date of the incident, Rafikabanu and her husband - accused No.2 had started living separately from her mother-in-law i.e. accused No.1 and the other two accused who were the sisters-in-law of the deceased.

It is the case of the NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED:
04/08/2025 undefined prosecution that, the accused used to frequently quarrel with the deceased on matters relating to dowry and gold ornaments and accordingly, she was being meted out with cruelty.

It is also the prosecution case that, the deceased was also taunted by all the accused that, she was not capable of bearing a child and despite one and a half years of her married life, she had not conceived and that she was not doing the household activities properly.

7. At the outset, before discussing the evidence relied upon in the present case and analysing the judgement rendered by the competent court, it would be appropriate to refer to the observations of the Apex Court regarding the scope of interference in acquittal appeals in the case of Chandrappa &
Ors. Vs. State of Karnataka reported in 2007 (4) SCC 415, wherein, the Apex Court has observed as under:
"Recently, in Kallu Vs. State of M.P. (2006) 10 SCC 313, this Court stated:
"While deciding an appeal against acquittal, the power of the Appellate Court is no less than the NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED:
04/08/2025 undefined power exercised while hearing appeals against conviction.

sentences.text: In both types of appeals, the power exists to review the entire evidence.

However, one State Of Gujarat vs Jebunisha Nanimiya Vora on 4 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19510981/

sentences.text: significant difference is that an order of acquittal will not be interfered with, by an appellate court, where the judgment of the trial court is based on evidence and the view taken is reasonable and plausible.
It will not reverse the decision of the trial court merely because a different view is possible.
The appellate court will also bear in mind that there is a presumption of innocence in favour of the accused and the accused is entitled to get the benefit of any doubt.
Further if it decides to interfere, it should assign reasons for differing with the decision of the trial court".

From the above decisions, in our considered view, the following general principles regarding powers of appellate Court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal emerge; (1) An appellate Court has full power to review, reappreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded; (2) The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 puts no limitation,
restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate Court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law;
(3) Various expressions, such as, 'substantial and compelling reasons', 'good and sufficient grounds',
'very strong circumstances', 'distorted conclusions', 'glaring mistakes', etc. are not intended to curtail extensive powers of an appellate Court in an appeal against acquittal.

Such phraseologies are more in the nature of 'flourishes of language' to emphasize the reluctance of an appellate Court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the Court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion.

(4) An appellate Court, however, must bear in mind NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption in favour of the accused.

Firstly, the presumption of innocence available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent court of law.
Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court.

(5) If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record,
the appellate court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial court.

7.1 In the case of Sanjeev v. State of Himachal Pradesh reported in 2022 (6) SCC 294, the Hon'ble Apex Court has held as under:
"7.

sentences.text: It is true that while deciding an appeal against acquittal, the Appellate Court has to reappreciate the evidence.

After re-appreciating the evidence, the first question that needs to be answered by the Appellate Court is whether the view taken by the Trial Court was a plausible view that could have been taken based on evidence on record.
Perusal of the impugned judgment of the High Court shows that this question has not been adverted to.

Appellate Court can interfere with the order of acquittal only if it is satisfied after reappreciating the evidence that the only possible conclusion was that the guilt of the accused had been established beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Appellate Court cannot overturn order of acquittal only on the ground that another view is possible.
In other words, the judgment of acquittal must be found to be perverse.
Unless the Appellate Court records such a finding, no interference can be made with the order of acquittal.
The High Court has ignored the well-settled principle that an order of acquittal further strengthens the presumption of innocence of the 326 [2024] 4 S.C.R. Digital Supreme Court Reports accused.
After having perused the judgment, we find that the High Court has not addressed itself on the main question.
7. The second error the High Court committed is found in paragraph 23 of the impugned judgment.

The High Court has gone to the extent of recording a finding that the appellants have failed to adduce evidence in their support, failed to examine the NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined defence witness and failed to establish falsity of the prosecution's version.
This concept of the burden of proof is entirely wrong.
Unless, under the relevant penal statute, there is a negative burden put on the accused or there is a reverse onus clause, the accused is not required to discharge any burden.
In a case where there is a statutory presumption, after the prosecution discharges initial burden, the burden of rebuttal may shift on the accused.

In the absence of the statutory provisions as above,
in this case, the burden was on the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
Therefore, the High Court's finding on the burden of proof is completely erroneous.
It is contrary to the law of the land.
Therefore, the appeal must succeed.
We set aside the judgment and order dated 14th December 2018 of the High Court and set aside the conviction of the appellants.
The judgment and order dated 5th July 1997 of the Trial Court is restored.

7.3 Thus, in case the appellate court agrees with the reasons and the opinion given by the competent court below, then the discussion of evidence at length is not necessary.

In light of the above settled principle of law laid down for acquittal appeals, we have briefly reppreciated the evidence led by the prosecution in the NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined present Sessions Case.
8.

It is required to be noted that, there are contradictions in the dying declarations of the deceased,
one before her mother and brother and the other before the Executive Magistrate.
In the oral dying declaration, she had stated that, she got up in the morning to go to the toilet.
At that time, her husband took a bottle of acid from the bathroom.
Her sisters-in-law and mother-in-law caught hold of her and her husband forcibly poured acid in her mouth.
After hearing her shouts, neighbours rushed to her house and thereafter, her husband and some boys of the street took her to the hospital.
8.1 In the dying declaration recorded before the Executive Magistrate below Exh. 67, the deceased mentioned that, due to the festival of Id, she and her husband had woken up early at about 4 am.

At that time, her mother-in-law and sisters-in-law complained about her not doing household chores properly and therefore, NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED:
04/08/2025 undefined the husband of deceased fetched the bottle of acid from other part of the house.
The mother-in-law and sisters-in- law of deceased
caught hold of her, and her husband forcibly poured 3/4th part of acid in her mouth.
She started vomiting and thereafter, her husband took her to the hospital.
9. Out of the six prosecution witnesses, P.W. 1 - Mehrajbibi Chandmiya Shaikh is the mother of the deceased and P.W. 2 - Abdulrehman Chandmiya Shaikh is the brother of the deceased.

Taking into consideration the oral dying declaration, which was given before the P.W. 1 & P.W. 2, it emerges that, P.W. 1 & P.W. 2 came to know about the incident in question from the deceased only when she told them about it in the hospital.
They did not have any personal knowledge about the incident or about any fights that allegedly used to happen between the accused and the deceased.

In the FIR below Exh. 37, the deceased stated that, she in fact tolerated the cruelty and torture meted out to her and had not informed any of NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED:
04/08/2025 undefined her family members.
Thus, P.W. 1 & P.W. 2 are only hearsay witnesses.
9.1 It is worthwhile to note that, the prosecution did not examine any independent witnesses.
The neighbours of the deceased or the person named Mansuri who was asked to inform the parents of the deceased about the incident were not examined by the prosecution.
If the case of the prosecution about dowry is to be believed, it cannot go unnoticed that, the articles of dowry were returned by the accused after the death of the deceased.

10. Considering the panchnama of the place of incident below Exh. 57, it is borne out that there were no acid bottles, either filled or empty, which would corroborate the say of the deceased that, the accused had forcibly poured acid into her mouth.

Even for the sake of assumption, considering that State Of Gujarat vs Jebunisha Nanimiya Vora on 4 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19510981/

Had she been administered acid forcibly, some acid would have spilled over either her body or the body of the accused persons.
11. The prosecution had not examined the doctor who had initially treated the deceased Rafikabanu.
There is no evidence on record to confirm that, the deceased was in fact administered acid or whether any poisonous medicine was consumed by the deceased herself.
Moreover, if the Vardhi received from the hospital below Exh. 56 is perused, it mentions the deceased having consumed some poisonous medicine.
On the other hand, the Vardhi below Exh. 63 refers to the involvement of the accused for administering acid to the deceased.
Thus, there are inconsistencies in both the vardhis.
12. P.W. 5 - Dr. Ravindra Bhinse was the Medical Officer who performed the post mortem.
He deposed below Exh. 69 that, the cause of death was due to NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined corrosive poisoning.
The postmortem report was signed by other two doctors also viz. Dr. F.R. Shah and Dr. Desai, but both of them have not been examined by the prosecution.
In view of the same, the prosecution has failed to prove the cause of death by acid beyond reasonable doubt.
13. In this regard, it shall be apposite to refer to a decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court rendered in the case of Sita Ram & Another vs. The State of Himachal Pradesh [[2025] 4 SCR 204].

After reproducing Section 32 of the Evidence Act in paragraph no. 48, it is held in paragraph no. 49 as under:
"49.
Whether a dying declaration should be believed or not would depend upon the circumstances of the case.
It is essentially a question of fact to be determined by the Court on the basis of the circumstances of each case.
As far as the credibility is concerned, it is just like the evidence given by a witness.
It is for the Court to decide whether to believe it or not and no rule can be laid down either that it should be believed or that it should not be believed.

Once it is believed, it is irrelevant and illogical to consider that it is not made on oath and that the maker has not been subjected to cross- NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined examination.
The oath, is administered simply with the object of making the witness speak the truth so that what he deposes may be believed.
The object of cross-examination is to test the veracity of the witness.
[See; Irfan @ Naka v. State of Uttar Pradesh reported in 2023 INSC 758]"

sentences.text: Now coming to the issue of the dying declaration.

There is no doubt regarding the wellsettled position of law that a dying declaration is an important piece of evidence and a conviction can be made by relying solely on a dying declaration alone as it holds immense importance in criminal law.
However, such reliance should be placed after ascertaining the quality of the dying declaration and considering the entire facts of a given case.

This Court in Uttam v. State of Maharashtra (2022) 8 SCC 576, with respect to inconsistent dying declarations, observed as follows:
"15.

entities.text: Uttam v. State of Maharashtra (2022) 8 SCC 576
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In cases involving multiple dying declarations made by the deceased, the question that arises for consideration is as to which of the said dying declarations ought to be believed by the court and what would be the guiding factors for arriving at a just and lawful conclusion.
The problem becomes all the more knotty when the dying declarations made by the deceased are found to be contradictory.

Faced with such a situation, the court would be expected to carefully scrutinise NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined the evidence to find out as to which of the dying declarations can be corroborated by other material evidence produced by the prosecution."

In other words, if a dying declaration is surrounded by doubt or there are inconsistent dying declarations by the deceased, then Courts must look for corroborative evidence to find out which dying declaration is to be believed.
This will depend upon the facts of the case and Courts are required to act cautiously in such cases.
The matter at hand is one such case.

In the present case, the deceased had given two statements which are totally different from her subsequent statements including the statement made before PW12 on 18.09.2008, which has been considered a dying declaration based on which the appellant has been convicted.
The first statement was made to the doctor (PW13) on the day of the incident itself where she told PW13 that the incident occurred while she was cooking.

On the same day, the second statement was made to the police constable (PW9)
where the deceased said the same thing i.e. she caught fire by accident while cooking in the kitchen."

13.2 In the present case, the prosecution had been unable to prove the cruelty or torture meted out to the deceased and that the accused were the perpetrators of the alleged crime by way of cogent evidence other than her dying declarations.
It is trite that, conviction can be based solely relying on the dying declaration, if it is found to be reliable and truthful.

However, at the same time, it NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined is also a settled law that, when dying declaration is doubtful of being voluntary and truthful, conviction cannot be based on same without corroboration, and that the court cannot in all cases presume, that dying person would not make a false statement.
13.3 However, as discussed hereinabove, the dying declarations record contradictions.

The testimonies of the family members of the deceased do not corroborate the version stated in the dying declaration, as they were not aware about the quarrels between the accused and the deceased,
till the time she told them after the alleged incident.

Moreover, neither does the postmortem report reveal any evidence with regard to injuries which would suggest any kind of cruelty meted out to the deceased nor does the report suggest that, the deceased was forcibly administered acid.

Upon overall appreciation of the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the defence put up by the accused, harmoniously with the findings recorded by us, we do not deem it fit to interfere with the reasonings assigned by the competent court.
The impugned judgment and order passed in Sessions Case No. 81 of 1994 is hereby confirmed.
15. Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed.

Such phraseologies are more in the nature of 'flourishes of language' to emphasize the reluctance of an appellate Court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the Court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion.
(4) An appellate Court, however, must bear in mind NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption in favour of the accused.
Firstly, the presumption of innocence available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent court of law.
Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court.
(5) If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record,
the appellate court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial court.
The High Court has ignored the well-settled principle that an order of acquittal further strengthens the presumption of innocence of the 326 [2024] 4 S.C.R. Digital Supreme Court Reports accused.
13. In this regard, it shall be apposite to refer to a decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court rendered in the case of Sita Ram & Another vs. The State of Himachal Pradesh [[2025] 4 SCR 204].
[See; Irfan @ Naka v. State of Uttar Pradesh reported in 2023 INSC 758]"
In other words, if a dying declaration is surrounded by doubt or there are inconsistent dying declarations by the deceased, then Courts must look for corroborative evidence to find out which dying declaration is to be believed.
This will depend upon the facts of the case and Courts are required to act cautiously in such cases.
The matter at hand is one such case.
In the present case, the deceased had given two statements which are totally different from her subsequent statements including the statement made before PW12 on 18.09.2008, which has been considered a dying declaration based on which the appellant has been convicted.
13.2 In the present case, the prosecution had been unable to prove the cruelty or torture meted out to the deceased and that the accused were the perpetrators of the alleged crime by way of cogent evidence other than her dying declarations.
It is trite that, conviction can be based solely relying on the dying declaration, if it is found to be reliable and truthful.
However, at the same time, it NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/1198/1999 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/08/2025 undefined is also a settled law that, when dying declaration is doubtful of being voluntary and truthful, conviction cannot be based on same without corroboration, and that the court cannot in all cases presume, that dying person would not make a false statement.
The testimonies of the family members of the deceased do not corroborate the version stated in the dying declaration, as they were not aware about the quarrels between the accused and the deceased,
till the time she told them after the alleged incident.
Moreover, neither does the postmortem report reveal any evidence with regard to injuries which would suggest any kind of cruelty meted out to the deceased nor does the report suggest that, the deceased was forcibly administered acid.

8 14.
Upon overall appreciation of the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the defence put up by the accused, harmoniously with the findings recorded by us, we do not deem it fit to interfere with the reasonings assigned by the competent court.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Therefore, the appeal must succeed.
We set aside the judgment and order dated 14th December 2018 of the High Court and set aside the conviction of the appellants.
The judgment and order dated 5th July 1997 of the Trial Court is restored.
The impugned judgment and order passed in Sessions Case No. 81 of 1994 is hereby confirmed.
15. Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed.
R & P, if any called for, to be sent back to the concerned Trial Court forthwith.
Bail bonds shall stand forfeited.
